stem:
Four minutes into an adult cardiac arrest, the CPR feedback device shows that the same person has compressed throughout. In the first two minutes the rate was 110/min at 5–6 cm with full recoil; now the rate is 85/min, depth is 4 cm, and end-tidal CO2 has fallen from 22 to 12 mmHg. A rhythm check is due in 20 seconds.

What should the team leader do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask the same compressor to push faster, aiming at 140/min
options.explanation: Fatigue is the cause, so urging the same person on rarely restores depth, and a rate of 140/min is too fast and shortens filling time.

options.label: B
options.text: Swap compressors at the check, targeting 100–120/min
options.explanation: Falling rate and depth with a parallel fall in end-tidal CO2 in a compressor who has worked for four minutes is fatigue. Change compressors at the rhythm check, with minimal pause, and target 100–120/min at 5–6 cm with full recoil.

options.label: C
options.text: Apply a mechanical CPR device now to restore quality
options.explanation: Mechanical devices are not used routinely, and fitting one interrupts compressions. A fresh compressor fixes fatigue at the check without that pause.

options.label: D
options.text: Check tube position, as end-tidal CO2 has fallen
options.explanation: Tube displacement causes an abrupt loss of the capnography trace. A gradual fall that tracks falling rate and depth points to poorer blood flow from tired compressions.

options.label: E
options.text: Increase the ventilation rate to raise end-tidal CO2
options.explanation: More ventilation does not correct poor compressions, and over-ventilation reduces venous return. End-tidal CO2 is falling because blood flow has fallen.

context: Compression quality falls with fatigue within minutes; swap compressors about every two minutes, or sooner if quality falls, and read a gradual fall in end-tidal CO2 alongside rate and depth as falling blood flow.
